strengths: Addresses a real, practical problem in deployed multilingual LLMs with clear motivation and problem formulation
Novel mechanistic analysis using SAEs showing causal link between high pre-activation values and code-switching
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 models, 6 benchmarks, 2 dataset sizes with proper statistical significance testing
Strong and consistent empirical results (>50% reduction in most cases, complete elimination in several scenarios) that outperform GRPO baseline
Thorough ablation studies on layer selection, feature selection, and threshold values with clear presentation of results
Practical method with no inference-time overhead that integrates easily into existing SFT pipelines
Good reproducibility documentation with detailed hyperparameters and implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core method is straightforward ReLU penalty on pre-activation values (Eq. 8), incremental over feasibility study in Section 3.2
Narrow evaluation scope limiting generalizability: only 3 languages with distinct writing systems; unclear performance on shared-alphabet languages; all models ≤9B parameters
Code-switching detection via Unicode character ranges is simplistic and may miss semantic appropriateness; no human evaluation of output quality

Heavy dependence on SAE availability: requires pre-trained SAEs (unavailable for Qwen-3, requiring in-house training); adds training-time computational overhead; no discussion of SAE quality or sensitivity
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices: selection of 'last two layers and first two features' lacks principled justification or ablation; limited sensitivity analysis for α_j and λ
Incomplete mechanistic understanding: paper demonstrates multi-layer/feature approaches work better but doesn't explain why; limited analysis of what model learns
Unfair baseline comparison: GRPO uses 10k samples while SASFT trains on 130k-230k samples; missing simpler baselines (prompt engineering, decoding constraints)
Reproducibility limited by proprietary training data and unreleased code; cannot recreate experiments or compare with future work
Mixed results on multilingual benchmarks with high variability across models and language pairs; some p-values >0.05 indicating lack of statistical significance in some conditions

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: unexpected code-switching is a real usability issue in multilingual LLMs
Insightful mechanistic analysis using SAEs, demonstrating correlation between high pre-activation values and code-switching (Figures 3-4)
Consistent improvements on primary metric: 50%+ code-switching reduction in 26/30 cases with statistical significance testing
Comprehensive experimental scope across 5 models and 3 languages with multiple dataset sizes
Preservation of multilingual capabilities shown on multiple benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, Flores-200, etc.)
Thorough ablations examining layer selection, feature selection, and threshold parameters
Clear presentation with detailed implementation details in appendices for reproducibility within constraints
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is a straightforward auxiliary loss term that directly applies existing SAE findings from Deng et al. [5]
Severely limited scope: only 3 languages tested despite claims of 'first in-depth analysis'; generalization to 100+ languages in modern LLMs is completely unclear
Script-based detection mechanism (GlotScript) fails for language pairs sharing alphabets (e.g., English-French) and is vulnerable to false positives from transliterations
All tested models are ≤9B parameters; effectiveness on 70B+ models where code-switching is prevalent in practice is unknown
Critical dependence on SAE quality with insufficient validation: for Qwen3, authors trained their own SAEs with no reported quality metrics or sensitivity analysis
Reproducibility severely compromised: proprietary training data cannot be released, code to be released later, and no public code available at submission
Artificial evaluation setup: SFT datasets constructed specifically to make code-switching 'more obvious' may not reflect natural user queries
Incomplete baseline comparisons: only standard SFT and poorly-tuned GRPO (10k samples); missing decoding-time interventions, constrained decoding, and prompt-based approaches
Lack of theoretical grounding: no formal justification for why lowering pre-activation values during training reduces inference code-switching; intuitive but not rigorously established
Unclear multi-language training strategy: experiments train separate models per target language; scalability to handling multiple language pairs simultaneously is not addressed

Inconsistent and unexplained results: GRPO sometimes outperforms SASFT (e.g., +43% for Korean); Table 2 shows benchmark degradations without adequate discussion; several non-significant p-values in Appendix E
Feature selection unjustified: why top-2 features? Figure 7 shows high variance; no systematic ablation provided
Missing human evaluation: no assessment of whether code-switching reduction produces natural, fluent outputs; relies only on automated metrics
Statistical rigor issues: some reported improvements suspiciously large (Llama-3.1-8B HumanEval: +17.7%); many comparisons show p > 0.05
SASFTEnhance variant (Appendix C) sometimes outperforms main method but is relegated to appendix without proper discussion

strengths: Clear problem formulation with practical significance - addresses real code-switching issue documented in community
Novel SAE-based mechanistic analysis revealing the link between language-specific feature pre-activation and code-switching, providing new interpretability insights
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 models, 3 languages, 6 multilingual benchmarks, with statistical significance testing and ablation studies
Consistent and substantial results: >50% code-switching reduction in 26/30 cases with 100% elimination in several scenarios, while maintaining or improving multilingual task performance
Practical method design with training-time intervention avoiding inference overhead, clearly applicable to real-world deployment
Thorough ablation studies examining layer selection (Fig. 6), feature selection (Fig. 7), and threshold settings (Table 3), demonstrating robustness
Well-written paper with clear presentation, detailed reproducibility information (Appendix D), and transparent experimental methodology
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core method is relatively straightforward (identify existing language features via SAEs, then add auxiliary ReLU loss), representing incremental application of Deng et al. (2025) rather than novel technique
Narrow evaluation scope: only 3 languages with distinct non-Latin scripts (Han, Cyrillic, Hangul); generalization to script-sharing language pairs unexplored; all models ≤9B parameters
Proprietary training data prevents full reproducibility and public verification despite detailed hyperparameter disclosure
Missing human evaluation despite framing as usability issue; script-based detection metric limited in applicability and doesn't assess semantic preservation or partial code-switching quality
Incomplete baseline comparison: only SFT and under-developed SFT+GRPO baselines; missing comparisons with alternative approaches (constrained decoding, prompt engineering, filtering)
SAE dependency not thoroughly analyzed: requires pre-trained SAEs (quality variation not studied), creates additional complexity beyond standard SFT, sensitivity to SAE hyperparameters unexplored

Method design choices appear heuristic: pre-estimated αⱼ thresholds rather than learned values, layer/feature selection uses grid search but methodology unclear, multi-layer choice justified only through ablation
Limited analysis of failure modes and outliers (e.g., Qwen3-8B Korean: SFT+GRPO +43%), no investigation of language-dependent performance differences (Russian vs Chinese in Fig. 7)

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear real-world impact documented across communities
Solid mechanistic analysis using SAEs that provides interpretable insights into code-switching behavior
Comprehensive experiments spanning 5 models, 3 languages, multiple dataset sizes, and 6 benchmarks
Consistent empirical results showing >50% reduction in code-switching while maintaining multilingual capabilities
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and promised code/data release
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating multi-layer and multi-feature approaches outperform single alternatives
Bidirectional causal evidence linking language feature pre-activation to code-switching (ablation and enhancement)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward application of existing SAE features with simple ReLU-based auxiliary loss
Dependence on external pre-trained SAEs limits applicability; requires SAE training for new models
Narrow scope: only 3 languages with distinct writing systems; unclear if method generalizes to shared-alphabet languages or low-resource languages

Scalability questions: all experiments on models ≤9B; performance on larger models unknown
Incomplete analysis: no qualitative examples, computational overhead comparison, or discussion of when SASFT might hurt performance

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement addressing a real issue in multilingual LLMs
Solid use of sparse autoencoders to provide mechanistic insights (Figures 3-4) linking language-specific features to code-switching
Comprehensive evaluation across 5 models and multiple languages with strong empirical results (>50% code-switching reduction)
Simple and practical method that doesn't require inference-time intervention
Thorough ablation studies examining layer and feature selection effects
Good reproducibility effort with detailed hyperparameters and appendices
Multi-layer analysis provides useful insights about feature behavior across network depth
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: method is a straightforward auxiliary loss applied to features identified by prior work (Deng et al. 2025); core contribution is incremental
Evaluation methodology concerns: script-based code-switching detection is coarse and doesn't handle same-script language pairs; no evaluation on Latin-script languages
Critical dependence on SAE quality not thoroughly analyzed; robustness study limited to Gemma models; computational overhead of training SAEs not discussed
Severely limited scope: only 3 non-Latin languages, models ≤9B parameters, trained on artificially balanced data; generalization to naturally distributed multilingual data unclear

Unclear design choices: threshold selection (α_j) procedure not precisely specified; feature/layer counts (2 features, 2 layers) not justified; different optimal λ values across models with no guidance
Incomplete causal analysis: feature enhancement experiments (Appendix K) only manipulate final layer at inference; connection to training-time constraints could be stronger
Missing comparisons: no comparison with alternative solutions (constrained decoding, prompt-based approaches); only weak baselines (GRPO, simple penalty); limited prior work discussion
Benchmark performance trade-offs not fully characterized: some degradations non-trivial (Qwen3-8B: -2.06% MMLU); no significance testing despite 8 runs; no pattern analysis across degradations
Incomplete analysis: paper doesn't explain why GRPO sometimes dramatically fails (+157% for Llama-3.1); no failure case analysis; insufficient investigation of deviations from expected behavior
Methodological questions: ReLU choice in Eq. 8 not justified; feature monolinguality metric (difference vs. ratio) not motivated; SFT+Penalty baseline relatively weak

strengths: Novel mechanistic analysis of unexpected code-switching using SAEs with clear causal evidence (ablation + enhancement experiments)
Strong consistent empirical results: >50% code-switching reduction in 23/30 cases with complete elimination in several scenarios, across 5 diverse model architectures
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple baselines, two dataset sizes, three languages, thorough ablations on layer/feature selection, robustness analysis across SAE configurations
Method well-grounded in mechanistic insights; practical solution that maintains/improves multilingual benchmark performance (6 benchmarks evaluated)
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, extensive appendix, promised code/data release
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of SAE-based constraints to SFT loss; novelty primarily in problem identification rather than methods

Narrow scope: only 3 target languages (all with distinct writing systems), unclear generalizability to shared-script languages (e.g., English-French); all models are base models <9B parameters, instruction-tuned models not evaluated
Dependence on SAE infrastructure: method requires pre-trained SAEs, limiting adoption; authors trained custom SAEs for Qwen3; no discussion of fallback strategies or behavior with inferior SAEs

Threshold design underspecified: choice of αⱼ values appears somewhat arbitrary; limited ablation (only vs. zero in Table 3), no sensitivity analysis, minimal guidance for practitioners setting thresholds on new languages

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: paper identifies that high feature pre-activation correlates with code-switching but not why models learn to activate irrelevant language features—limits insights for more fundamental solutions

Multi-layer training mechanism not analyzed: why multi-layer outperforms single-layer unexplained; potential side effects on other language pairs not explored; analysis of impact on linguistic representations missing

Evaluation constraints: script-based detection only reliable for distinct writing systems; binary metric doesn't measure severity; no error bars or confidence intervals reported; single experimental runs with 8× repetitions only

Limited baseline coverage: SFT+Penalty is author-proposed; no comparison with simpler approaches (token penalties, vocabulary filtering) or other linguistically motivated methods; GRPO comparison limited to single variant

Applicability constraints: requires multilingual training data (limits low-resource languages); behavior on intentional code-switching/naturally code-mixed text unexplored; computational overhead not discussed; only base models tested
Missing failure case analysis: no discussion of scenarios where SASFT underperforms; generalization to unseen code-switching patterns and different prompting styles not studied
